extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: Microsoft Common Objects in Context (MS COCO) is a large-scale dataset designed to advance object recognition within the broader context of scene understanding. It contains 328,000 images depicting complex everyday scenes with 2.5 million labeled instances across 91 common 'thing' object categories, annotated with per-instance segmentation masks and five captions per image.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick, "Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context," in ECCV, 2014.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Candidate images were collected from Flickr by querying for pairs of object categories, pairs of scene and object categories, and single categories. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers filtered candidates via a dedicated grid interface to remove invalid or iconic images.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Flickr images and metadata uploaded by amateur photographers.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were filtered using crowdsourcing to remove iconic images. Near-duplicate images were explicitly detected and removed using GIST descriptors, and images were grouped by photographer and capture date to prevent near-duplicates across train/val/test splits.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations followed a multi-stage pipeline: (1) Category Labeling: workers used a hierarchical interface of 11 super-categories and dragged category icons to label presence and one instance location; (2) Instance Spotting: workers placed crosses on up to 10 instances of a detected category using a magnifying glass; (3) Instance Segmentation: workers produced precise polygonal segmentations using an adapted OpenSurfaces interface; if more than 10-15 instances were present, remaining instances were annotated collectively via crowd painting; (4) Segmentation Verification: segmentations were verified by multiple workers; (5) Five natural language caption descriptions were added per image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Category labeling quality was evaluated by comparing AMT worker consensus (union of responses) to ground truth established by majority vote among expert workers (co-authors), demonstrating that 8 AMT workers attained over 99% recall. Leave-one-out evaluation was used to evaluate worker precision and recall, and work from underperforming annotators was discarded. For instance segmentation, workers were required to pass a qualification training task; segmentations were then judged by 3 to 5 workers, requiring at least 4 of 5 positive votes to be retained.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling; 8 workers per image for instance spotting; 1 worker per segmented instance; 3 to 5 workers per instance for segmentation verification; 5 written caption descriptions per image.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was released in two phases: the 2014 release (82,783 train, 40,504 val, and 40,775 test images with 80 categories) and the cumulative 2015 release (165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images across 91 categories). Train and validation annotations are released publicly while test annotations are retained for automatic benchmarking on an evaluation server. The dataset website http://mscoco.org/ hosts continuous updates.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors highlight canonical/iconic viewpoint bias present in prior object recognition datasets and intentionally sample non-iconic, contextual, and cluttered compositions; category frequencies exhibit natural variations in co-occurrence and instance count.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Only 'thing' categories are segmented, excluding 'stuff' background categories. For dense groups exceeding 10-15 instances of a category (e.g., crowds of people, truckloads of bananas), instances are marked as composite crowd segments rather than individually segmented. Eleven categories were omitted from segmentation in the initial 2014 release due to high frequency, ambiguity, confusion with related classes, or scarcity.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and benchmarking of computer vision algorithms for object classification, bounding-box object detection, instance-level semantic segmentation, contextual reasoning, and image captioning.
